prize_parts.citation: For the development of palladium-catalyzed carbon-nitrogen cross-coupling

statement.case_for: Palladium-catalyzed C-N cross-coupling is the cleanest case on the table: a clearly defined discovery, a clearly bounded pair of originators, three decades of independent confirmation and very wide practical use in pharmaceutical, agrochemical and materials synthesis. Buchwald and Hartwig built the general catalyst/ligand systems and the mechanistic understanding behind them, in parallel and independently. Three of eight members (Chabes, Somfai and I) ranked it first with the same two-laureate configuration, which is unusual agreement on both topic and attribution in a field where most other candidates have unresolved credit disputes. The prize would reward chemistry in the core sense, not a neighbouring discipline.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is redundancy with the 2010 cross-coupling prize (Heck, Negishi, Suzuki): a sceptic can call C-N coupling an extension of the same principle rather than a new concept, and Kosugi's earlier tin-amide work leaves a residual priority question. Also, opening support is only three first places, and it did not reach the top three of the other five members, so it may be a strongly held but narrow preference rather than a broad one.

responses.point: Daniel ranks targeted protein degradation (B026) first as a new drug modality, with Crews, Deshaies and Ciulli, and notes the hard omission of Handa and others under the three-name cap.
responses.response: I agree B026 is a genuinely original chemical idea and the most widely supported candidate (six top-three placements). My reservation is attribution and maturity: PROTACs and molecular glues are two strands with different heroes (Crews/Deshaies versus Handa/Ito on cereblon), and no degrader is approved. A three-name prize would split a story that the field itself treats as two. I would not block it later, but it needs more time or a cleaner formulation than we have now, which is why I keep it as an alternative and not as my preferred choice.

responses.point: Heiner ranks massively parallel sequencing (B037) first, as chemistry-driven technology (reversible terminators, clonal arrays) with exceptional impact, with Balasubramanian, Klenerman and Mayer.
responses.response: The impact is not in doubt, and I accept that the Solexa terminator chemistry is real chemistry. My disagreement is about attribution and fit. The sequencing platform emerged from several competing routes (Rothberg, Ju, Mayer), and a third laureate is a judgement call that I cannot defend as clearly as the Buchwald-Hartwig pair. Part of the credit also lies with engineering and commercial development, which makes the chemical claim less sharp. I would give it more weight than my opening ranking did, but I would not put it above a candidate with a well-defined and uncontested pair of originators.

responses.point: Andrei also ranks B065 first with Buchwald and Hartwig, but flags the overlap with the 2010 cross-coupling prize and the Kosugi precursor.
responses.response: We agree on the configuration. On the 2010 overlap, I think the difference is substantive: the C-N coupling needed a new ligand-controlled mechanistic framework, with amide-bound palladium intermediates and difficult reductive elimination, not just a different nucleophile. Heck, Negishi and Suzuki were about C-C bonds with organometallic partners. The Kosugi issue is a citation-wording matter, which a phrase like 'general catalytic' resolves, and it does not justify a third name.

responses.point: Xiaodong ranks halide perovskite photovoltaics (B056) first, for the efficiency leap, the new materials class and its broad chemistry impact, while acknowledging that credit among Miyasaka, Park, Snaith, Kanatzidis, Gratzel and Seok is contested.
responses.response: I respect the originality and the scale of the field. Yet two issues weigh for me. The stability and toxicity questions are not marginal, they decide whether the discovery will matter as technology, and a prize now may be premature. Second, the credit is spread over six or more groups, so any three names would be openly arguable. I would wait on B056 until the stability picture is clearer, and that is a timing judgement and not a scientific objection.

responses.point: Peter ranks B065 first and sees recognition as overdue, with a fair two-person prize; he puts photoredox catalysis (B033) second while leaving MacMillan out.
responses.response: I agree on B065 and its maturity. On photoredox, I qualify my own earlier ranking: leaving out MacMillan because he is already a laureate is defensible, but the result is a trio whose credit is diffuse (Yoon, Stephenson, Nicewicz, with Konig, Melchiorre and Fukuzumi all with claims). I place it behind C-N coupling and would not combine it with B065 in a single prize, because two synthetic-methodology awards close together would narrow the prize's breadth.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will see C-N coupling as separate enough from the 2010 cross-coupling prize.
Whether Kosugi should be reflected in the citation wording, even if not as a laureate.
Whether a second part is needed to broaden the prize (for example B026 or B004) or whether a single two-laureate prize is better.
Whether the committee will see protein degradation (B026) as mature enough this year given no approved PROTAC drug yet.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile for B065. My profile lists a connection with Arieh Warshel and with the Uppsala ribosome/RNA community, and none of the shortlisted candidates involves them, though B032 (energy landscapes, protein folding) is close to my biomolecular simulation field and I would note it if it became a serious contender.
